key_insight: Large language models should not be entrusted alone to attribute or situate knowledge: they frequently produce plausible but unsupported claims and lack reliable provenance, so attribution must be engineered outside the model.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the risk that language models generate assertions without correct sourcing or contextual grounding (misattribution, hallucination, and loss of provenance), and shows that attribution and situating knowledge require system-level design, evaluation, and oversight rather than being left to model output alone.
method: Systematic diagnostic evaluation of language models' ability to name sources and place claims in context, revealing frequent errors and inconsistencies in attribution.
Analyses that differentiate types of failure (hallucinated sources, context collapse, overconfident but unsupported statements) to show where models fail to situate knowledge.

Propose practical design principles and workflows: integrate retrieval and provenance metadata, uncertainty calibration, and human-in-the-loop checks to ensure correct attribution and situating of knowledge.
impact: For practitioners, this work shifts focus from only improving model parameters to building systems that surface provenance, verify claims, and enforce contextual grounding—reducing misinformation risk and improving trustworthiness in deployed AI.
visual_elements: Flow diagram showing an LA (language model) pipeline augmented with retrieval, provenance metadata, and human-in-the-loop verification.
Bar chart or heatmap comparing model-attributed claims vs verified-source claims to illustrate misattribution rates.
Icon set representing types of failure (hallucination, misattribution, context loss) with short examples.
Checklist / decision tree visual for engineers: when to accept model claim, when to fetch sources, when to escalate to human review.
paper_title: Attributing and situating knowledge cannot be left to language models
